notes.summary: Statistical inference draws conclusions about a population from a sample. Paper 2 covers estimation (point and interval estimates, and what makes a good estimator) and testing of hypotheses (null and alternative hypotheses, Type I and Type II errors, level of significance, power, and the z, t, χ² and F tests). Most questions are either definitions or one-line computations of a test statistic, a confidence interval or degrees of freedom.

concepts.title: Point and interval estimation
concepts.body:
• An estimator is a rule (formula) using the sample, such as x̄. An estimate is the number it gives for one sample, such as x̄ = 52.
  • Point estimate: a single value for the parameter.
  • Interval estimate (confidence interval): a range that is expected to contain the parameter with a stated confidence, such as 95%.
  • Methods of finding estimators: method of moments, maximum likelihood (MLE), least squares.

concepts.title: Properties of a good estimator
concepts.body:
PropertyMeaningExample
UnbiasedE(T) = θ: on average it hits the true valuex̄ for μ; s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1) for σ²; sample proportion p for P
ConsistentT gets closer to θ as n grows (Var → 0 for an unbiased T)x̄ for μ
EfficientSmallest variance among unbiased estimatorsFor a normal population, the mean is more efficient than the median
SufficientUses all the information in the sample about θΣx for the Poisson λ or the binomial p
  • Σ(x − x̄)²/n is a biased estimator of σ²; dividing by n − 1 removes the bias.
  • An unbiased estimator with the least variance is called MVUE. The Cramér–Rao inequality gives the lowest possible variance.
  • Sufficiency is checked with the Fisher–Neyman factorisation theorem.
  • Maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and, for large samples, efficient; they need not be unbiased.

concepts.title: Confidence intervals
concepts.body:

Proportion (n large)p ± z × √(pq/n)
Confidencez

  • Higher confidence gives a wider interval; a larger n gives a narrower one.
  • Width = 2 × z × σ/√n. Margin of error = z × σ/√n.

Example: n = 100, x̄ = 50, σ = 10. 95% CI = 50 ± 1.96 × 1 = (48.04, 51.96).

concepts.title: Hypotheses and significance
concepts.body:
• Null hypothesis H0: the claim of no difference or no effect, tested directly (μ = 50).
  • Alternative hypothesis H1: what we accept if H0 is rejected. μ ≠ 50 gives a two-tailed test; μ > 50 or μ < 50 gives a one-tailed (right or left) test.
  • Test statistic: the value computed from the sample (z, t, χ², F).
  • Critical region (rejection region): values of the statistic that lead to rejecting H0.
  • Level of significance α: the probability of the critical region when H0 is true, usually 5% or 1%.
  • p-value: the probability, under H0, of a result at least as extreme as the one seen. Reject H0 if p-value ≤ α.
αTwo-tailed zOne-tailed z

concepts.title: Errors and power
concepts.body:
H0 trueH0 false
Reject H0Type I error (probability α)Correct decision (probability 1 − β = power)
Accept H0Correct decision (probability 1 − α)Type II error (probability β)
  • Type I error is also called the producer's risk (a good lot is rejected); Type II is the consumer's risk (a bad lot is accepted).
  • Power = 1 − β = P(reject H0 when it is false).
  • For a fixed n, lowering α raises β. Increasing n can lower both.

concepts.title: Large-sample z tests
concepts.body:
Testz statistic
One mean(x̄ − μ0) / (σ/√n)
Two means(x̄1 − x̄2) / √(σ1²/n1 + σ2²/n2)
One proportion(p − P0) / √(P0Q0/n)
Two proportions(p1 − p2) / √(p̂q̂(1/n1 + 1/n2)), p̂ = pooled proportion

Used when n is large (usually n > 30) or σ is known. Compare |z| with 1.96 (5%) or 2.58 (1%) for a two-tailed test.

concepts.title: t tests (small samples)
concepts.body:
• Used when the population is normal, σ is unknown and n is small.
  • One sample: t = (x̄ − μ0) / (s/√n), with s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1); df = n − 1.
  • Two independent samples (equal variances): t = (x̄1 − x̄2) / (sp√(1/n1 + 1/n2)); df = n1 + n2 − 2.
  • Paired t test (before and after on the same units): work with the differences d; df = n − 1.
  • Testing a correlation coefficient: t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²), df = n − 2.
  • The t distribution is symmetric about 0, has heavier tails than the normal, and approaches the normal as df grows. Its variance is ν/(ν − 2) for ν > 2.

concepts.title: Chi-square tests
concepts.body:
• χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E. It is never negative.
  • Goodness of fit: df = (number of classes) − 1 − (parameters estimated from the data).
  • Independence of attributes in an r × c contingency table: E = row total × column total ÷ grand total; df = (r − 1)(c − 1). A 2 × 2 table has 1 df (Yates' correction is used when cell counts are small).
  • Variance of a normal population: χ² = (n − 1)s²/σ0² with n − 1 df.
  • Each expected frequency should be at least 5; merge classes otherwise.
  • A χ² variable with ν df has mean ν and variance 2ν. Its curve is positively skewed.

concepts.title: F test
concepts.body:
• Tests whether two normal populations have equal variances: F = s1² / s2², with the larger variance on top so F ≥ 1.
  • Degrees of freedom: (n1 − 1, n2 − 1), numerator first.
  • F is also the test statistic in analysis of variance.
  • F is never negative. The square of t with ν df is F with (1, ν) df.

varieties.name: Properties of estimators
varieties.how: Unbiased: E(T) = θ. Consistent: improves as n grows. Efficient: least variance. Sufficient: uses all the information. Divide by n − 1 for an unbiased variance.

example.q: A sample gives 2, 4 and 6. Find the unbiased estimate of the population variance.

varieties.name: Confidence intervals
varieties.how: Interval = estimate ± (critical value × standard error). Pick z = 1.645, 1.96 or 2.576 for 90%, 95% or 99%.

example.q: A sample of 36 has mean 80. The population SD is 12. Find the 99% confidence interval for the mean (z = 2.58).

varieties.name: Hypotheses, errors and power
varieties.how: Type I = reject a true H<sub>0</sub> (α). Type II = accept a false H<sub>0</sub> (β). Power = 1 − β.

example.q: A test has α = 0.05 and β = 0.20. What is its power?

varieties.name: Large-sample z tests
varieties.how: z = (statistic − hypothesised value) ÷ standard error. Compare |z| with the critical value.

example.q: A coin is tossed 100 times and shows 60 heads. Test whether it is fair at the 5% level.
steps: |z| = 2 > 1.96, so reject H<sub>0</sub>: the coin is not fair.

varieties.name: t tests and their degrees of freedom
varieties.how: One sample: t = (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n), df n − 1. Two samples: df n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub> − 2. Paired: df n − 1.

example.q: A sample of 16 has mean 53 and s = 8. Find t for testing H<sub>0</sub>: μ = 50, and its degrees of freedom.

varieties.name: Chi-square tests
varieties.how: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. df = k − 1 for goodness of fit (minus estimated parameters) and (r − 1)(c − 1) for a contingency table.

example.q: A die is thrown 60 times. Faces 1 to 6 appear 8, 12, 9, 11, 6 and 14 times. Find χ² for testing that the die is fair.

varieties.name: F test for variances
varieties.how: F = larger s² ÷ smaller s², with df (n − 1) of the numerator sample first.

example.q: Sample 1: n = 11, s² = 20. Sample 2: n = 9, s² = 8. Find F and its degrees of freedom.

tips: "Not equal" in H<sub>1</sub> means two-tailed; "more than" or "less than" means one-tailed.
Degrees of freedom: subtract one for each quantity estimated from the data.
Halving the margin of error needs four times the sample size.
χ² and F are never negative; t and z can be negative.
If the p-value is smaller than α, reject H<sub>0</sub>.
traps: Type I is rejecting a true H<sub>0</sub>; Type II is accepting a false one. Do not swap them.
For an unbiased variance divide by n − 1, not n.
In a contingency table df = (r − 1)(c − 1), not rc − 1.
Accepting H<sub>0</sub> does not prove it true; it only means the data are not strong enough to reject it.

questions.q: A Type I error is committed when:
options: H<sub>0</sub> is accepted when it is false
H<sub>0</sub> is rejected when it is true
H<sub>1</sub> is rejected when it is false
questions.solution: Type I error = rejecting a true null hypothesis. Its probability is α, the level of significance.

questions.q: For a 95% confidence interval using the normal distribution, the critical value z is:
questions.solution: Two-tailed 95%: 2.5% in each tail, so z = 1.96. (1.645 is for 90%, 2.576 for 99%.)
